source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Answer the common interview question about Redis data types. Lead with the classic five core types named by the frozen source entities—String, List, Hash, Set and Sorted Set (ZSet)—then clearly distinguish newer or specialized Redis data types such as Streams and bitmap/bitfield/geospatial/probabilistic structures instead of claiming Redis has exactly five types in current releases.

sources.title: Redis Docs: Data types
anchors: current Redis documentation includes Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted sets and Streams among its data types
current Redis documentation also lists specialized structures such as bitfields, bitmaps, geospatial indexes and other newer data types
therefore an interview answer should not present 'exactly five types' as a timeless statement about current Redis

sources.title: Redis Docs: Strings
anchors: Redis strings are sequences of bytes and are the simplest value type associated with a key
strings are used for caching and also support counters and bitwise-related operations

sources.title: Redis Docs: Hashes
anchors: Redis hashes are collections of field-value pairs
hashes are suitable for representing simple objects and groupings of counters

sources.title: Redis Docs: Lists
anchors: Redis lists are ordered sequences supporting pushes/pops at the ends and range access
typical use cases include recent-item sequences and producer-consumer patterns

sources.title: Redis Docs: Sets
anchors: Redis sets model unique unordered members and support membership/set operations
membership-style workloads are a core set use case

sources.title: Redis Docs: Sorted sets
anchors: Redis sorted sets associate unique members with scores and maintain ordering by score
sorted sets support rank/range style access

sources.title: Redis Docs: Streams
anchors: Redis Streams are append-only log-like data structures
Streams support IDs, range access and consumer groups
XADD and core Stream commands date from Redis 5.0

claims.text: For the frozen 2024-style interview wording and source entities, the direct baseline answer is the classic five: String, List, Hash, Set and Sorted Set (ZSet).

Current Redis documentation contains additional data types and specialized structures, including Streams and bitmap/bitfield/geospatial/probabilistic/newer structures, so 'Redis has exactly five data types' is not a version-independent current statement.

The five classic types differ primarily by data model: String is a byte sequence, List is ordered sequence data, Hash is field-value records, Set is unique unordered membership data, and Sorted Set is unique members ordered by score.

Streams are a first-class log-like data structure with IDs and consumer-group semantics and should be mentioned as a modern extension rather than silently folded into the classic-five interview mnemonic.

writer_constraints: Answer the source wording directly by naming String, List, Hash, Set and Sorted Set/ZSet first; those are also the entities explicitly preserved by the Canonical context.
Do not say current Redis has exactly five data types. After the classic five, mention Streams and specialized/newer structures with a version-aware boundary.
Explain each classic type by data model plus one representative use case; do not turn the answer into a command catalog.

Keep Bitmap and Bitfield semantics distinct from claiming they are one of the historical five; Redis documentation treats them as data-type/features layered around string storage and command semantics.

Do not invent internal encoding details (ziplist/listpack/quicklist/intset/hashtable thresholds) unless separately sourced and version-pinned; this Canonical asks what types exist, not implementation internals.
Do not fabricate production hit rates, memory savings or company-specific Redis usage.
